To date, the evidences of the costs of RA patients remained insufficient in mainland of China. Compared to the total costs of per RA patient as $3,826 published by Xu et al. in 2014 [11] and $2,410 (RMB) published by Hu et al. in 2017 [12], our estimation of 41,971 CNY (or $6,507 based on the 2021 RMB to US dollar exchange rate) of total cost per patient were increased by 0.7 times or 1.7 times respectively. On the one hand, the most important changes in RA treatment were reflected in the treatment strategy in the recent decade, advocating early T2T approach as a guiding principle, which entails intensive treatment and regular follow-up with the goal of achieving low disease activity or clinical remission [25–27]. And advanced approaches emphasize on the importance of attaining at least 50% improvement in disease activity within 3 months of drug administration [28]. On the other hand, with the introduction of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors, followed thereafter by application of interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) inhibitors, T-lymphocyte co-stimulation inhibitors (Abatacept), B cell depletion (Rituximab), as well as Janus Kinase (JAK) inhibitors, the treatment of RA in China has gradually begun to enter the targeted era [29]. In our study, nearly one-quarter of the patients receiving biologic or target synthetic therapies, which was only 3% reported by Hu et al [12]. All of these reduced the comorbidity and mortality of RA and help more RA patients to achieve the drug-maintained remission. But they also increased the costs related to treatment. In addition, the majority of total costs were direct cost, in which more than 50% for medication expense, which was consistent with the previously studies in China [11, 12]. According to the data of the National Bureau of Statistics of China, the annual per capita disposable income was 36,883 CNY in 2022 [18]. It indicated that the annual per patient's direct costs (32,448 CNY) estimated in our study accounted for approximately 88% of per capita disposable income. Moreover, only 17% of RA patients reported the hospitalization during the last year in our study, so the outpatient expenditure was main composition of cost. Although nearly 67.5% of patients self-reported to have medical insurance, the outpatient expense was reimbursed in a very low proportion slightly varied by provinces in China [30]. Cao et al. published in 2025 reported the $907.78 per-capita cost of RA patients based on database of health insurance in urban of China in 2013–2017 years. Due to the fact that the patient's out-of-pocket expenses and patients uncovered in medical insurance were not considered, it might underestimate the costs of RA in real-word of mainland of China [3]. Overall, the results in our study implied most of patients had to pay the expenses from out-of-the pocket by themselves or their family, which induce to have to face financial hardship due to RA with long-term duration and incurable features, especially for those living in close to or below the poverty line families with sever disease and/or comorbidities.

However, there were still limitations in our study. Firstly, the indirect costs for patients estimated using the human capital approach, but not included the costs of premature retirement by RA and intangible costs, that might underestimate the indirect costs. Secondly, RA patients frequently carried multiple comorbidities, not all of which were RA-related. Because we captured their total annual healthcare spending, our per-patient costs might overestimate costs attributable solely to RA. Thirdly, the estimation of costs was based on data collected by patient-self reported and there might be recall bias. In order to improve the accuracy as much as possible, we only invited the patients whose clinical records were updated by the clinicians who they visited during last 30 days, and participants were requested to recall the expense information of this recent visit in detail and frequency of visits last year. Moreover, at the initial stage, 53 patients were randomly selected to collect information repeatedly in two weeks to assess agreement of information. Fourthly, given the cross-sectional design, we couldn’t exclude the possibility of reverse causation or residual confounding. Therefore, the observed associations between the influence factors and expenditures of RA warrant confirmation in further prospective cohort studies. Lastly, considered the overall response rate of only 7%, our cross-sectional study was susceptible to non-response bias. Although IPW mitigated imbalances in observed characteristics, residual confounding from unmeasured factors (such as income, health-seeking behaviors, et al.) might persist, potentially limiting the external validity of our findings to the wider RA population.
log.response: However, our study still had several limitations. First, indirect costs for patients were estimated using the human capital approach, but this approach did not include costs associated with premature retirement due to RA or intangible costs; therefore, indirect costs may have been underestimated. Second, RA patients frequently had multiple comorbidities, not all of which were related to RA. Because we captured total annual healthcare spending, our per-patient costs may have overestimated costs attributable solely to RA. Third, cost estimates were based on patient-reported data, which may have introduced recall bias. To maximize accuracy, we invited only patients whose clinical records had been updated by the clinicians they had visited within the previous 30 days, and participants were asked to recall detailed expenditure information for this recent visit and their frequency of visits in the previous year. Moreover, at the initial stage, 53 patients were randomly selected to provide information repeatedly over a two-week period to assess the consistency of the information. Fourth, given the cross-sectional design, we could not rule out reverse causation or residual confounding. Therefore, the observed associations between influencing factors and RA-related expenditures warrant confirmation in future prospective cohort studies. Finally, considering the overall response rate of only 7%, our cross-sectional study may have been susceptible to non-response bias. Although IPW mitigated imbalances in observed characteristics, residual confounding from unmeasured factors (such as income and health-seeking behaviors) may have persisted, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to the broader RA population.
